summary.text: The coefficient of determination, R², is the proportion of the variation in the dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variables.
It measures how well a model reproduces observed outcomes: a perfect match gives R²=1, and a simple baseline model gives R²=0.
With ordinary least squares it never decreases as variables are added, so adjusted R² was devised to penalize extra variables.

facts.label: Perfect fit
facts.value: Modeled values matching observed values exactly give R² of 1

facts.label: Usual range
facts.value: Smaller than 1 and usually greater than 0

facts.label: Negative values
facts.value: Can arise when predictions were not fitted to those data

facts.label: Adding variables
facts.value: Under ordinary least squares, R² never decreases

facts.label: Adjusted R²
facts.value: Penalizes the statistic as extra variables are included

items.prompt: Two models predict house prices from the same data. Model A has an R² of 0.9 and model B has 0.4. What does that tell us?

options.label: Model B reproduces the observed prices better
Model A reproduces the observed prices better
The models cannot be compared at all
Model A uses more variables than model B

items.explain: R² measures how well observed outcomes are replicated by the model, and R²=1 is the best case where they match exactly.

items.prompt: An analyst keeps adding irrelevant factors, such as a model's first letter, to a regression just to push R² up. What happens, and what is the remedy?

options.label: R² falls, so extra variables are self-correcting
R² stays exactly the same however many are added
R² will not fall, so adjusted R² is used, which penalizes extra variables
R² becomes negative as soon as a factor is irrelevant

items.explain: With ordinary least squares, R² never decreases as variables are added, which rewards kitchen-sink regression. Adjusted R² penalizes the statistic for extra variables.

items.prompt: Someone computes R² using predictions that were not derived by fitting a model to those data, and gets a negative number. What does that mean?

options.label: The data must contain a recording mistake somewhere
The model must be a perfect fit to the data
The correlation between the variables is negative
The data's average fits better than the predictions do

items.explain: Negative values can arise when predictions are not from a fitting procedure on those data, and then the mean of the data fits the outcomes better than the predicted values do.

items.prompt: Every point lies exactly on the model's predictions, so the leftover squared error is zero. What is R²?

options.label: Exactly 0
Exactly 1, the best case
Exactly 0.5
Negative

items.explain: In the best case the modeled values exactly match the observed values, which gives SS_res = 0 and R²=1.

items.prompt: In a simple linear regression with an intercept, the sample correlation between predictor and outcome is 0.5. What is R²?
items.explain: In simple linear regression with an intercept, r² is simply the square of the sample correlation coefficient, and 0.5 squared is 0.25.

items.prompt: A manager sees an error figure in dollars whose scale means little to her. Why might R² be easier to judge?

options.label: It can be shown as a percentage, unlike measures with arbitrary range
It is always computed in dollars as well as units
It cannot be affected by a poor fit to the data
It needs no model of any kind to be calculated

items.explain: R² can be more intuitively informative than error measures such as MSE and RMSE because it can be expressed as a percentage, whereas those have arbitrary range.

paragraphs.heading: A score for how well a model fits
paragraphs.text: The coefficient of determination, written R² and read as R squared, tells you what share of the variation in an outcome can be predicted from the variables used to explain it. It measures how closely a model reproduces the outcomes that were actually observed. In short, it is a measure of goodness of fit. It is used both for models built to predict and for models built to test hypotheses.

paragraphs.heading: The ends of the scale
paragraphs.text: If the model's values match every observed value exactly, R² equals 1. A baseline model that always predicts the mean of the observed data scores R² of 0. Because R² can be stated as a percentage, it can be easier to read than error measures such as MSE or RMSE, whose ranges are arbitrary.

paragraphs.heading: Link to correlation
paragraphs.text: In simple linear regression with an intercept, r² is just the square of the sample correlation coefficient r. When further predictors are added, R² becomes the squared coefficient of multiple correlation. In both of these cases it is always below 1 and usually above 0. Several different definitions of R² exist, and they only sometimes agree.

paragraphs.heading: When R² goes negative
paragraphs.text: R² can drop below zero. This can happen when the predictions were not produced by fitting a model to those same data. It can also happen after fitting, for example in a linear regression with no intercept or when a nonlinear function is fitted. A negative value means that simply using the mean of the data would fit the outcomes better than the model does.

paragraphs.heading: Why more variables mislead
paragraphs.text: When a model is fitted by ordinary least squares, R² never falls as you add variables; it can only stay level or rise. That invites a bad habit of piling in variables just to push R² up. Suppose you predict a car's sales from its mileage, price and engine power. You could add the first letter of its name or the height of its lead engineer, and R² would not drop and would likely creep up by chance alone.

paragraphs.heading: The adjusted version
paragraphs.text: This problem leads to a second measure, adjusted R². It is read in nearly the same way as R², but it is penalized as extra variables enter the model. R² values can be worked out for any kind of predictive model, even one with no statistical basis.
